title: The Merchant's Fair Bargain
summary: An apprentice merchant in an old Arabian trading town is tempted to overcharge a traveler who doesn't know the fair price, but learns from his honest master that fair dealing builds lasting trust and success.
poll: A merchant should always try to get the highest price possible, even from a customer who doesn't know any better.

versions.title: The Merchant's Fair Bargain
versions.text:
Long ago, there was a market town. A boy named Salim lived there.

Salim helped a merchant. His name was Ammar. Ammar sold cloth and dates. Salim wanted to sell things, too.

One day, a man came to the market. He came from far away. He did not know the fair price.

Salim had an idea. "I could ask for more," he thought. The man would not know. Salim could keep the coins.

But Ammar saw his face. Ammar knew what he was thinking. Ammar shook his head.

Ammar told the man the fair price. It was the same for all. The man smiled. He said thanks.

Later, Ammar talked to Salim. "Be fair," he said. "Be honest. It makes people glad. They come back."

"If you are not fair, they will not trust you," said Ammar. "They will not come back."

Salim thought about this. From that day on, Salim was fair. He was honest, too.

versions.title: The Merchant's Fair Bargain
versions.text:
Long ago, there was a busy market town. A boy named Salim lived there.

Salim helped a merchant named Ammar. Ammar sold cloth and dates. Salim was his helper. He wanted to learn to trade, too.

One hot day, a traveler came to the market. He came from far away. He did not know the fair price of cloth.

Salim had an idea. "I could ask for more coins," he thought. "He will not know the real price." Salim could keep the extra coins.

But Ammar saw the look on Salim's face. He knew what Salim was thinking. Ammar gave a small shake of his head.

Ammar told the traveler the fair price. It was the same price for all. The traveler smiled and said thanks.

Later, Ammar sat with Salim. "A good merchant must be fair and honest," he said. "A fair price makes buyers glad. Glad buyers come back again."

"An unfair merchant may gain more coins just once," said Ammar. "But people stop trusting him. They will not come back."

Salim thought hard about this. From that day on, Salim always gave a fair price. He wanted people to trust him, too.

versions.title: The Merchant's Fair Bargain
versions.text:
Long ago, there was a busy market town in Arabia. A boy named Salim lived there with his family, and he loved to watch the traders at work.

Salim helped a merchant named Ammar. Ammar sold cloth and dates in the market, and people came from many towns to buy from him. Salim was his apprentice. He hoped to become a merchant himself one day.

One hot afternoon, a tired traveler came to the market. He had come from a far-off land, and his clothes were covered in dust from the road. He did not know the fair price of the cloth sold here.

Salim had an idea. "I could ask him for more coins," he thought. "He will never know the real price." Salim could keep the extra coins for himself, and no one would ever find out.

But Ammar noticed the look on Salim's face. He knew exactly what Salim was thinking, because he had once been tempted the very same way. Ammar gave a small, quiet shake of his head.

Ammar told the traveler the fair price. It was the very same price he gave to every single customer, rich or poor. The traveler smiled with relief and thanked him warmly.

Later, Ammar sat down beside Salim. "A good merchant must always be fair and honest," he said. "A fair price makes customers glad, and glad customers always come back again."

"An unfair merchant might gain a few extra coins just once," Ammar explained. "But soon people stop trusting him completely, and they will never come back to his shop."

Salim thought hard about these wise words. From that day on, Salim always gave a fair price to everyone who visited the shop. He wanted people to trust him, just as they trusted Ammar.

versions.title: The Merchant's Fair Bargain
versions.text:
Long ago, in a busy trading town in Arabia, there lived a boy named Salim. He loved to watch the merchants bargain in the crowded market square.

Salim worked as an apprentice to a merchant named Ammar. Ammar was known for the fine cloth and sweet dates he sold. Salim hoped that one day he would run his own stall, too.

One hot afternoon, a tired traveler arrived at the market. He had come from a distant land, and dust from the road still clung to his clothes. He was a stranger here, so he did not know the fair price of cloth.

An idea formed in Salim's mind. "I could charge him more," he thought, "and he would never know the difference." No one would notice if Salim kept the extra coins for himself.

But Ammar noticed the look on Salim's face. He remembered being tempted the same way when he was young. Without a word, Ammar gave a slow shake of his head.

Ammar then named the traveler the same fair price he gave every customer. Relief spread across the traveler's face, and he thanked Ammar warmly before going on his way.

Later that evening, Ammar sat down with his apprentice. "A good merchant must deal fairly," he explained. "A fair price keeps customers satisfied, and satisfied customers return again, often bringing their friends."

"An unfair merchant might earn a quick profit just once," Ammar continued. "But word travels fast through a market town. Once people stop trusting a merchant, they rarely come back."

Salim thought about these words as he closed the stall for the night. From that day on, he always offered a fair price to every customer. He wanted to earn the same trust and good reputation that people gave Ammar.

versions.title: The Merchant's Fair Bargain
versions.text:
Long ago, in a busy trading town in Arabia, there lived a boy named Salim. He loved to watch the merchants bargaining and haggling in the crowded market square.

Salim worked as an apprentice to a merchant named Ammar. Ammar was well known for the fine cloth and sweet dates he sold. Salim hoped that one day he would run his own stall in the market, too.

One hot afternoon, a tired traveler arrived at the market. He had journeyed from a distant land, and dust from the long road still clung to his clothes. Because he was a stranger here, he had no idea what a fair price for cloth should be.

An idea quickly formed in Salim's mind. "I could charge him a higher price," he thought, "and he would never know the difference." No one would notice if Salim quietly kept the extra coins for himself.

But Ammar had noticed the look on Salim's face. He remembered being tempted in the same way when he was a young apprentice. Without saying a word, Ammar gave a slow, deliberate shake of his head.

Ammar then named the traveler the same fair price he offered every customer who entered his stall. Relief spread across the traveler's tired face, and he thanked Ammar warmly before continuing on his journey.

Later that evening, after the stall had closed, Ammar sat down with his apprentice. "A good merchant must always deal fairly," he explained. "A fair price keeps customers satisfied, and satisfied customers return again, often bringing their friends along with them."

"An unfair merchant might earn a quick profit just once," Ammar continued, "but word travels fast through a small market town. Once people stop trusting a merchant, they rarely ever return to his stall."

Salim thought carefully about these words as he helped close up for the night. From that day forward, he always offered a fair price to every customer, determined to build the same lasting trust and reputation that people placed in Ammar.

Years later, when Salim finally opened his own stall, travelers often said that his prices never changed, whether they were wealthy merchants or simple strangers passing through.

versions.title: The Merchant's Fair Bargain
versions.text:
Long ago, in a bustling trading town somewhere in Arabia, there lived a boy named Salim, who spent countless hours observing the merchants haggle over prices in the crowded market square, fascinated by the rhythm of the negotiations.

Salim worked as an apprentice to a merchant named Ammar, who had earned a solid reputation throughout the region for the exceptional cloth and sweet dates he sold at a consistently fair and honest price. Salim hoped that one day he would operate his own stall, applying the same careful judgment he admired in his master.

One scorching afternoon, an exhausted traveler arrived at the market. He had journeyed from a distant land, and dust from the long road still clung stubbornly to his worn garments. Because he was a complete stranger to this town, he had no way of knowing what a fair price for cloth should reasonably be.

An idea quickly formed in Salim's mind. "I could charge him a considerably higher price," he thought to himself, "and he would never know the difference." No one would ever notice if Salim quietly pocketed the extra coins for himself.

Ammar, however, had already noticed the calculating look crossing Salim's face, because he vividly remembered being tempted in precisely the same way during his own years as a young apprentice. Without uttering a single word, he gave a slow, deliberate shake of his head.

Ammar then quoted the traveler the exact same fair price he offered every customer who approached his stall, regardless of how wealthy or impoverished they appeared to be. Visible relief spread across the traveler's weary face, and he thanked Ammar warmly before continuing on his long journey homeward.

Later that evening, once the stall had finally closed for the day, Ammar sat down with his apprentice to discuss what had transpired earlier. "A reputable merchant must deal fairly with every single customer," he explained patiently. "A fair price keeps customers genuinely satisfied, and satisfied customers return again and again, frequently bringing their friends and relatives along with them."

"An unscrupulous merchant might manage to earn a handful of extra coins on one occasion," Ammar continued, "but word travels remarkably quickly through a small market town such as ours. Once customers stop trusting a merchant entirely, they will rarely, if ever, return to purchase from his stall again." A merchant who exploits a stranger's ignorance may gain some quick commerce for a single day, Ammar added, but only a trustworthy merchant can sustain a business built on real integrity.

Salim reflected carefully on these wise words as he helped close up the stall for the night. From that day forward, he consistently offered a fair price to every customer, determined to cultivate the same enduring trust and sterling reputation that people placed in Ammar without hesitation.

Years later, after Salim had finally opened his own stall in the market, travelers from faraway lands frequently remarked that his prices never seemed to fluctuate, whether they were affluent merchants or simple strangers passing through the town for the very first time.

An idea quickly formed in Salim's mind, tempting and persuasive. "I could charge him a considerably higher price," he thought to himself, weighing the possibility with uncomfortable care, "and he would almost certainly never know the difference, since he has nothing to compare it against." Once customers stop trusting a merchant entirely, they will rarely, if ever, return to purchase from his stall again, no matter how low he later drops his prices in a belated attempt to win them back." A merchant who deliberately exploits a stranger's unfamiliarity with local prices might gain a brief surge of commerce for a single day, Ammar added thoughtfully, but only a genuinely trustworthy merchant can sustain a thriving business that is firmly and permanently built on lasting, unshakable integrity rather than on any momentary advantage gained at someone else's expense.

Salim reflected carefully on these wise words as he helped close up the stall for the night, turning them over in his mind long after the market square had grown quiet and still beneath the darkening evening sky overhead. From that day forward, he consistently offered a fair price to every customer who approached him, determined to cultivate the same enduring trust and sterling reputation that people placed in Ammar without the slightest hesitation or doubt.

Years later, after Salim had finally opened his own modest stall in the very same market, travelers from faraway lands frequently remarked that his prices never seemed to fluctuate in the slightest, whether they were affluent merchants bargaining confidently or simple strangers passing through the town for the very first time, entirely unfamiliar with local customs and prevailing prices.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of the story?
options: Fair dealing, rather than short-term profit gained by exploiting a customer's ignorance, is what sustains a merchant's reputation and long-term success.
Traveling merchants from distant lands always pay noticeably more than local customers in every Arabian market and shop, since they carry more coins and gold.
Ammar's apprentice, Salim, eventually becomes far wealthier than his master by learning to bargain aggressively with each and every customer.
Honest merchants in old Arabia were required by strict law to charge perfectly identical prices to every single buyer in the market.

wrong.B: The story never claims travelers always pay more; Ammar deliberately refuses to do this.
wrong.C: The story never compares Salim's and Ammar's wealth.

He is tempted to overcharge the traveler, who does not know the fair local price

wrong.B: Ammar quotes the traveler the usual fair price, not a raised one.
wrong.C: Ammar says nothing out loud to the traveler about Salim.

wrong.C: Exploiting someone raises unfair advantage, not lowers prices kindly.

questions.stem: Based on Ammar's explanation, why is a reputation for integrity more valuable than a single unfair profit?
options: Because a reputation for integrity brings repeat customers and lasting commerce, while one unfair sale destroys trust permanently.

wrong.D: Taxes are never mentioned in the story.

questions.stem: What can readers infer about Ammar's own past from his reaction to Salim's temptation?

questions.stem: What is the ultimate cause of Ammar's lasting success as a merchant, according to the story?

His long-standing habit of quietly charging more money to his wealthier customers

questions.stem: Why does the author end the story by describing Salim's own stall years later?

To show that the lesson of fair, trustworthy commerce lasted and shaped Salim's own future choices
To explain in detail how Salim became wealthier than Ammar himself in only a few years
To suggest that prices in this market always rise over time, because merchants grow greedy and sell less cloth

wrong.A: Salim's prices stay fair and unchanged, showing he did not abandon the lesson.
wrong.C: The story never compares Salim's and Ammar's wealth.
wrong.D: The story says Salim's prices never changed, not that they rose.
